106.title: Fatigue

patient_voice.chief_complaint: I'm feeling really weak and tired. I'm scared something is seriously wrong.
patient_voice.history: I just started feeling unwell. I have a fever and I don't know why.
patient_voice.pain: I have a dull ache all over my body.

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with fatigue.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
No acute rash; capillary refill and perfusion assessed.
106.hpi_narrative: Clinical Summary: This patient was admitted with neutropenic fever. Tumor lysis syndrome was considered. The patient was started on IV fluids, antibiotics, and supportive care. The patient was admitted to the ICU for close monitoring and further management. The patient was noted to have a high ANC, >500, but the patient was still at risk for infection. It is important to understand the severity of the patient's neutropenia. In this case, the patient is severely neutropenic.

108.hpi_narrative:
Initial History

Reason(s) for visit: Abdominal Pain
History of present Illness:
A 22-year-old female presents to the emergency room with abdominal pain, lethargy, and vomiting x2 days. Her vomiting is non-bloody. Her abdominal pain is diffuse, which she rates as a 6/10. She also claims to have had an increased appetite prior to having these symptoms. She also claims that she’s been developing blurry vision, dizziness, and drowsiness. She also states that she is having increased urination

Past Medical History

Past Medical History: None
Current medications: Birth control
Allergies: None
Vaccinations: The patient received her childhood vaccinations. She has never received any HPV vaccines.
Women's health: The patient cannot remember when her last pap smear was done.
Family History: The patient has a brother with Diabetes. 

Social History:
Marital/Family: Single. She is an undergraduate student at a local university.
Personal habits: The patient denies smoking. She drinks socially. She smoked marijuana "a few times" with her friends. She denies other illicit drugs or misuse of medications. Occupation/educational: She is a student at a local university
Recreational: She plays the piano and sings in a band. 

Review of systems:
General: See HPI
Skin: Her skin is dry. 
HEENT: Her throat is dry. 
Cardiorespiratory: She feels that her heart is beating faster.
Gastrointestinal: See HPI
Genitourinary: See HPI
Neuropsychiatric: See HPI

111.title: Shortness of Breath

patient_voice.chief_complaint: I'm really scared. I can't breathe well at all.
patient_voice.history: I had an injury a few days ago, and now I feel terrible.
patient_voice.pain: It feels like there's pressure in my chest.

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with shortness of breath.
Skin rash morphology and distribution documented.
111.hpi_narrative:
Differentiate: CHF, pneumonia, embolism, aspiration, heart failure, pneumonia, systemic lupus erythematosus.

The patient has fat embolism syndrome (FES). This typically occurs from hours to days after an initial injury that allows globules (typically from bone marrow) to enter the blood stream. Long bones such as a femur are common causes of FES. FES can also cause respiratory distress, and information on risk factors should be taken, including the patient's history.

The patient has many metabolic abnormalities; the lab results and thrombocytopenia which are very common in fat embolism syndrome. He also has metabolic acidosis, increased level of BUN, and increased creatinine which are also commonly seen in fat embolism syndrome.

Diagnosis is mainly clinical as imaging is not very reliable. Chest x-ray and CT scans can be misleading in this case. The patient could have an abnormal CT scan, but this will take too much time to administer. The patient will require immediate supportive treatment.

A commonly used criteria is the Gurd and Wilson criteria for fat embolism to help clinicians determine if the patient is suffering from a fat embolism. The major criteria are:

1. Pyrexia > 38.0 °C
2. Central nervous system depression
3. Petechiae

There are other criteria, but these will not be listed. The patient, positive in the minor criteria, has tachycardia more than 100 beats per minute, and his globules in plasma in the urine. At least two positive major criteria plus one minor criteria is suggestive of fat embolism. In this case, the patient has safety problems, hypotension, and tachycardia; all of these in turn is a concern order on the EMS.

Treatment is supportive. The patient should be transferred to the ICU, intubated, put on a ventilator. The patient should be given fluids. Albumin therapy is considered experimental and corticosteroids administration is controversial, so the majority treatment is just supportive. One thing to avoid is heparin/anticoagulant treatment. This has shown benefit in fat embolism cases, and it increases the risk of hemorrhage.

111.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Fat Embolism Syndrome.

115.title: Agitation

patient_voice.chief_complaint: I feel really out of control and scared. I don't know what's happening to me.
patient_voice.history: I was just sitting there, and then everything got overwhelming.
patient_voice.pain: I feel like my head is spinning and my heart is racing.

No acute rash; capillary refill and perfusion assessed.
115.hpi_narrative:
Differential diagnosis: Substance induced psychotic disorder, Schizophrenia, Psychosis secondary to a medical condition, Delirium, Epileptic seizures, Electrolyte disturbance

This case is similar to the schizophrenia cases, but this case focuses just on correctly treating acute agitation which is a common occurrence in most emergency departments. As the patient has already assaulted a staff member, IV medication is needed for rapid medication onset to be effective. A typical regimen is colloquially called the 5-2-1 regimen 5 mg of Halidol (Haloperidol), 2 mg of IM Ativan (Lorazepam), and 1 mg of IM Cogentin. As Cogentin is key here, an alternative is 2.5 mg of Halidol, 2 mg of IM Ativan (Lorazepam), and 5 mg of IM Benadryl (Diphenhydramine). Droperidol has its limitations as it is not the best choice. Once the patient is treated, the vital signs can be completed. There can be medical causes of acute agitation which should be ruled out, but given the age of the patient and his history in the hospital, it is unlikely that a medical diagnosis will be determined in this case.

Other second-generation antipsychotics are available for the distressed patient including: IM Olanzapine (Zyprexa), IM Aripiprazole (Abilify), or IM Ziprasidone (Geodon). Halidol is the most commonly administered in hospital emergency settings due to the availability of IM administration along with Lorazepam (Ativan) along with Cogentin or Benadryl to avoid a potential EPS (Extrapyramidal Syndrome) and dyskinesias. This is an area which is being studied as newer antipsychotics will treat agitation as well as psychosis.

117.hpi_narrative:
Initial History

Reason(s) for visit: Chest pain; respiratory distress
History of present Illness:
The patient, a 65-year-old accountant, is brought to the emergency department by ambulance from the trucking company, where he works. Ten minutes prior to the ambulance’s arrival, the patient developed excruciating, sharp pain on the right side of his chest accompanied by marked respiratory distress. He rates the pain as an 8 on a 10-point scale. The pain increases on respiration, and he is unable to answer questions. A coworker who accompanied the patient to the hospital says that this has never happened to the patient in the past. Coworker mentions patient has a past medical history of emphysema and asthma. Oxygen was administered during transport.
117.clinical_tip: Until proven otherwise, treat unstable chest pain as ACS.
117.objective: Rule out life threats. ECG within 10 minutes.

118.hpi_narrative: Rhabdomyolysis is a condition characterized by the breakdown of muscle tissue, leading to the release of muscle fiber contents into the bloodstream. This can result in serious complications, including acute kidney injury. The management of rhabdomyolysis involves identifying the underlying cause, providing supportive care, and monitoring for complications. It is important to maintain adequate hydration and to monitor renal function closely. In some cases, additional treatments such as bicarbonate therapy may be indicated to prevent kidney injury.

119.hpi_narrative: Differential: Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis, Retropharyngeal abscess, Epiglottitis, Lemierre Syndrome, Lateral Pharyngeal Abscess, Other Bacterial pharyngitis. This patient has viral pharyngitis. The exact virus will not be determined in the case as it typically is not determined in real life. The main point of the case is to not over-treat. It is important to rule out a Group A Streptococcal infection by doing a rapid group A strep test. If negative, give only symptomatic relief with pain medications (ibuprofen or Acetaminophen) along with salt water gargles which has been shown to help. No other interventions are necessary in this case. In time, the patient will begin to feel better. If you give antibiotics, you would fail the case. Antibiotics can cause harm in viral infections do not help and have led to antibiotic resistance.

120.title: Sore Throat

patient_voice.chief_complaint: I'm really scared. My throat hurts so much!
patient_voice.history: I can't swallow well. It hurts a lot.
patient_voice.pain: It feels like my throat is on fire.

120.hpi_narrative:
Differential: Group C and G Streptococcal Pharyngitis, Retropharyngeal Abscess, Epiglottitis, Infectious mononucleosis, Viral Pharyngitis.

Group A Streptococcus (GAS) is the most common cause of bacterial pharyngitis in children. The physical exam and history are consistent with a bacterial pharyngitis. The patient does not have any real symptoms such as congestion or cough. The patient also has a characteristic purplish rash along with tonsillar edema. A rapid strep test should be ordered. It will take too long to make the right decision regarding whether to administer antibiotics or not if the 24 hour strep test is done.

Penicillin/Amoxicillin are the treatment of choice for GAS. Alternatives include Cephalosporins (Cephalexin, Ceftriaxone, Cefuroxime, Cefdinir, Meropenem, Azithromycin or Clindamycin).

Acetaminophen or Tylenol can be administered to treat pain and fever. Once antibiotics are given, the patient will feel better. The patient should be counseled to take the entire regimen of antibiotics to avoid developing antibiotic resistance.

123.hpi_narrative:
The patient has classical symptoms of DVT. The risk factors for DVT include: obesity, tenderness at area of interest, pitting edema, calf swelling 3cm larger than the other leg, and distal swelling of the leg. Use of the Wells Score.

The D-Dimer results will be elevated in DVT, but this would be a high probability due to risk factors including a positive PVT. A calf ultrasound (duplex) should be done to confirm the diagnosis. The patient should be put on anticoagulants. The options for anticoagulants for DVT are: LMWH heparin (Lovenox) / Warfarin (Coumadin) CR Lovenox / dalteparin CR Lovenox / edoxaban OR Rivaroxaban monotherapy OR Apixaban Monotherapy.

124.hpi_narrative:
Initial History

Reason(s) for visit: Chest pain; respiratory distress
History of present Illness:
The patient, a 65-year-old accountant, is brought to the emergency department by ambulance from the trucking company, where he works. Ten minutes prior to the ambulance’s arrival, the patient developed excruciating, sharp pain on the right side of his chest accompanied by marked respiratory distress. He rates the pain as an 8 on a 10-point scale. The pain increases on respiration, and he is unable to answer questions. A coworker who accompanied the patient to the hospital says that this has never happened to the patient in the past. Coworker mentions patient has a past medical history of emphysema and asthma. Oxygen was administered during transport.
124.clinical_tip: Until proven otherwise, treat unstable chest pain as ACS.

patient_voice.chief_complaint: I'm really scared about my bleeding. I don't want to get hurt.
patient_voice.history: I had a virus recently, and now I have these spots and bleeding.
patient_voice.pain: My gums bleed when I brush my teeth.

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with rash.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
Skin rash morphology and distribution documented.
127.hpi_narrative:
This patient in this case has immune thrombocytopenia (ITP). The patient most likely developed ITP after having a recent viral infection. ITP patients will have platelet counts less than 100,000/microl, with a normal white blood cell count and hemoglobin. The majority of children develop ITP after a recent viral illness. The patient has gingival bleeding and petechiae. This would classify the patient as a grade I/IV between moderate and severe. The patient will require treatment with either glucocorticoids, IVIG or both. 

The patient at risk for potentially severe bleeding if injured, so the patient should be counseled to avoid contact sports as well as to avoid antiplatelet medications like Aspirin and NSAIDs. Depending on the treatment choice, the patient can be treated either inpatient or outpatient. Once the patient gets treatment, he will improve.

Family History: The patient has a brother with Diabetes.

133.hpi_narrative:
Differential: Chronic Nonspecific Back Pain, Fibromyalgia, Vertebral Compression Fracture, Sacroiliac joint infection, Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis.

The patient has Ankylosing Spondylitis. The patient has classic symptoms of Ankylosing Spondylitis which include back pain, morning stiffness, and a history of psoriasis. These increase the likelihood of having Spondylitis.

Initial evaluation should be a physical exam focusing on extremities and eyes for iritis/uveitis. Other tests include HLA-B27, and X-rays of the pelvis and spine.

Once the diagnosis of Ankylosing Spondylitis is made, treatment should be with a TNF inhibitors Etanercept, Infliximab, Adalimumab (not an order on the USMLE), but TNF inhibitors in 1 inhibitors are not yet available as orders on the USMLE which include Secukinumab and Ixekizumab. Interleukin 17 inhibitors are also treatment options for Ankylosing Spondylitis.

Once the correct treatment is given, the patient will begin to feel better after a week, and the case will end.

Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
Warm skin with fever; no purpura on initial survey.
134.hpi_narrative:
Differential: Testicular Torsion, Trauma, Inguinal Hernia, Testicular cancer, Referred pain.

The patient has Acute Epididymitis. Due to the age of the patient and his risk sexual partners, his acute Acute Epididymitis is most likely from an infectious source. Imaging is not required in this case as the Physical exam shows tenderness and swelling of the epididymis. The patient’s clinical picture reflects the quality would be negative in testicular torsion.

The most common infectious causes of Acute Epididymitis are N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. These should be tested for, but they are commonly negative in those who do not have urinary tract symptoms such as in this case. As the patient practices safe sex, co-infection between the two could be the cause of his Acute Epididymitis.

This case can be treated as an outpatient. The patient can be treated with oral antibiotics, NSAIDS, application of ice to the scrotum, and scrotal elevation.

The antibiotic choice in this case would be ceftriaxone plus a fluoroquinolone to cover all the possible culprits of gonorrhea, chlamydia, and rectal flora.

After 48 hours of treatment, the patient will begin to feel better, and the case will end. The patient should be counseled on safe sex practices.

patient_voice.chief_complaint: I'm really tired all the time and I feel weak. I'm scared about what's happening to me.

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with fatigue.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Altered mental status with attention and command-following documented.
No acute rash; capillary refill and perfusion assessed.
138.hpi_narrative:
Differential: Acute Kidney Disease, Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD), Medullary Cystic Kidney Disease, IgA Nephropathy, Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis, Fabry disease.

The patient has end stage renal failure likely from diabetes mellitus and hypertension. The patient is not active with a creatinine of 9.4. The patient has primary metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap with full exploratory compensation. The patient has too many metabolic abnormalities to be treated as an outpatient (including a possibility of 6), the patient will require inpatient hospitalization and dialysis.

Nephrology should be consulted to help with the management of the patient. A kidney transplant will be needed as a long-term solution.

Indications for dialysis include needing nutritional status, fatigue, muscle mass, and cognitive impairment, hyperkalemia, refractory acidosis. The patient in this case easily meets these criteria.

Once the patient is put on dialysis, the patient will begin to feel better, and the case will end.

We have received emails regarding why this patient requires hemodialysis. The patient is symptomatic and has a creatinine of 9.4. The calculated eGFR based on a 60-year-old would be mL/min/1.73m2. The patient is having memory problems. Your doctor, and is very well right; the patient will require dialysis. Dialysis indications are the following - eGFR is < 15 mL/min/1.73m2, uremic encephalopathy (the patient has been having episodes of confusion which is likely due to uremic encephalopathy), cognitive impairment, hyperkalemia, fatigue and malaise, persistent volume overload, and declining nutritional status. The patient clearly meets these criteria. Efforts to treat the hyperkalemia with various medications prior to hemodialysis are not needed as hemodialysis will treat the hyperkalemia and other metabolic problems.

139.title: Lip Lesion
139.diagnosis: Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Lip

patient_voice.chief_complaint: I'm really scared about this lip lesion. What if it's serious?
patient_voice.history: I noticed a bump on my lip that hasn't gone away. It looks different.
patient_voice.pain: It feels tender and sometimes itchy.

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with lip lesion.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
No acute rash; capillary refill and perfusion assessed.
139.hpi_narrative: The patient has squamous cell carcinoma of the lip. This is a fairly straight forward case. You diagnose by a biopsy and then remove the tumor by consulting dermatology to perform Mohs surgery. Mohs surgery tends to be the gold standard for removing facial tumors as it minimizes tissue loss. The Mohs surgeon will remove a layer where the tumor was located and take the tissue, dye it, and look at the histology of the removed tissue. If there are still cancer cells in the specimen, the Mohs surgeon will go back and remove more of the lesion and then there is no more cancer. The patient will wait in the office while the Mohs surgeon looks at the tissue, so that the surgeon can remove more tissue if necessary. Mohs surgery will preserve the most tissue and have the best cosmetic outcome which is important to most patients. Mohs surgery is an outpatient procedure and can be done with local anesthetic. Once the surgery is completed, the case will end.

142.title: Seizures

patient_voice.chief_complaint: I'm scared and feel really weak. I don't understand what's happening.
patient_voice.history: I was feeding fine, but then I started feeling strange. My movements are weird.
patient_voice.pain: I have a strange feeling in my stomach and my head hurts.

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with seizures.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Neurologic exam focused on mental status and focal deficits.
No acute rash; capillary refill and perfusion assessed.
142.hpi_narrative:
Differential: Beta-ketothiolase deficiency, Glycine encephalopathy, Methylmalonic acidemia, Propionic acidemia.

The patient has the signs of classic Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD) which include irritability, poor feeding, bicycling movements, focal dystonia, and seizures. The are 5 types of MSUD (Classic, Intermediate, Intermittent, Thiamine-responsive, and E3-deficient). Classic MSUD is the most common. The amino acid levels are given in two because these orders are not present on the USMLE at this time. There are no orders for serum or urine levels of leucine, valine, isoleucine, or leucine. However, you must put together that high amino acid levels with the presentation to come up with the MSUD diagnosis.

The treatment for MSUD is a no-protein/low-protein diet. This specialized diet would be life-long much like PKU. The patient would not be able to breast-feed and would need a non-branched-chain amino acids (meaning low, leucine, valine, isoleucine) formula. There is no specific diet for non-branched-chain amino acid diet, so a low-protein/protein diet is utilized. It is recommended that all patients with MSUD be treated with a thiamine to see if the patient has the Thiamine-responsive type. If there is no improvement after 4 weeks, then the thiamine treatment can be discontinued.

A potential long term treatment of MSUD is liver transplantation. As the patient is only a week old, this discussion would happen at a later time and would depend on the outcome of diet modification.

Note that in this case, the CBC/ CMP will be normal which is not abnormal as the patient seems to be suffering more neurological damage than metabolic issues. However, metabolic decompensation is a possibility, so the patient should be followed closely. Admitting to the hospital/ICU is appropriate until the patient can be stabilized and amino acid levels returned to normal levels. MSUD is more severe than PKU as this can lead to death.

152.hpi_narrative:
Initial History

Reason(s) for visit: Headache
History of present Illness:
A 55-year-old female with a past medical history of hypertension presents to your office with a an occipital headache, mild vertigo, and a tendency to fall when walking for 6 days. She states that she never had any problems walking or being off-balance. Eight days ago, she stated that she had a pink rash on her arms and torso and felt feverish. The rash improved after a couple days, but the headache and tendency to fall persisted. She had nausea, but she denied any vomiting. She feels weak and "under the weather."  She denies travel, but went hiking 2 weeks ago nearby her house which she routinely does every summer. She denies any history of migraines. She will occasionally get a tension headache which she will treat with Ibuprofen. She has never had a headache that has lasted this long. She denies any trauma to her head. She denies any sick contacts. She denies any recent antibiotic use.  She is very concerned about her symptoms.

PMH:
Past Medical History: Hypertension. The patient recently had a colonoscopy screening which was normal. 
Current medications: HCTZ 25mg PO daily
Allergies: None
Vaccinations: Received Childhood vaccinations.
Women's health: The patient cannot remember when her last pap smear was done.
Family History:
Her father has a history of Hypertension and died of a stroke. Her mother has no health problems and is still living.

Social History:
Marital/Family: She is married with one child. She lives in Gaithersburg, Maryland.
Personal habits: The patient denies smoking. She lives an active lifestyle. She drinks alcohol socially. She denies use of illegal drugs or misuse of medications.
Occupation/educational: She works as a public relations specialist. She is a college graduate with a BS in communication.
Recreational: The patient enjoys to bike and hike. She loves the outdoors and spends as much time as she is able.

Review of systems:
General: See HPI
Skin: See HPI
HEENT: Negative
Cardiorespiratory: Negative
Gastrointestinal: See HPI
Genitourinary: Negative
Neuropsychiatric: See HPI

The rash improved after a couple days, but the headache and tendency to fall persisted. She had nausea, but she denied any vomiting. She feels weak and "under the weather." She denies travel, but went hiking 2 weeks ago nearby her house which she routinely does every summer. She denies any history of migraines. She will occasionally get a tension headache which she will treat with Ibuprofen. She has never had a headache that has lasted this long. She denies any trauma to her head. She denies any sick contacts. She denies any recent antibiotic use. She is very concerned about her symptoms. PMH: Past Medical History: Hypertension. The patient recently had a colonoscopy screening which was normal. Current medications: HCTZ 25mg PO daily Allergies: None Vaccinations: Received Childhood vaccinations. Women's health: The patient cannot remember when her last pap smear was done. Family History: Her father has a history of Hypertension and died of a stroke. Her mother has no health problems and is still living. Social History: Marital/Family: She is married with one child. She lives in Gaithersburg, Maryland. Personal habits: The patient denies smoking. She lives an active lifestyle. She drinks alcohol socially. She denies use of illegal drugs or misuse of medications. Occupation/educational: She works as a public relations specialist. She is a college graduate with a BS in communication. Recreational: The patient enjoys to bike and hike. She loves the outdoors and spends as much time as she is able. 161.hpi_narrative:
Initial History

Reason(s) for visit: Headache
History of present Illness:
A 55-year-old female with a past medical history of hypertension presents to your office with a an occipital headache, mild vertigo, and a tendency to fall when walking for 6 days. She states that she never had any problems walking or being off-balance. Eight days ago, she stated that she had a pink rash on her arms and torso and felt feverish. The rash improved after a couple days, but the headache and tendency to fall persisted. She had nausea, but she denied any vomiting. She feels weak and "under the weather."  She denies travel, but went hiking 2 weeks ago nearby her house which she routinely does every summer. She denies any history of migraines. She will occasionally get a tension headache which she will treat with Ibuprofen. She has never had a headache that has lasted this long. She denies any trauma to her head. She denies any sick contacts. She denies any recent antibiotic use.  She is very concerned about her symptoms.

PMH:
Past Medical History: Hypertension. The patient recently had a colonoscopy screening which was normal. 
Current medications: HCTZ 25mg PO daily
Allergies: None
Vaccinations: Received Childhood vaccinations.
Women's health: The patient cannot remember when her last pap smear was done.
Family History:
Her father has a history of Hypertension and died of a stroke. Her mother has no health problems and is still living.

Social History:
Marital/Family: She is married with one child. She lives in Gaithersburg, Maryland.
Personal habits: The patient denies smoking. She lives an active lifestyle. She drinks alcohol socially. She denies use of illegal drugs or misuse of medications.
Occupation/educational: She works as a public relations specialist. She is a college graduate with a BS in communication.
Recreational: The patient enjoys to bike and hike. She loves the outdoors and spends as much time as she is able.

Review of systems:
General: See HPI
Skin: See HPI
HEENT: Negative
Cardiorespiratory: Negative
Gastrointestinal: See HPI
Genitourinary: Negative
Neuropsychiatric: See HPI

164.hpi_narrative:
Initial History

Reason(s) for visit: Pelvic pain
History of present Illness:
This is a 20-year-old previously healthy female presenting to your office complaining of pelvic pain for the last month. She rates the pain as a constant 7/10 sharp pain which worsens when she moves. She was encouraged by her boyfriend to come to you because she is having extreme pain during sex. Ibuprofen "takes the edge off." The pain is severe enough that she reports having difficulty sleeping. Her pain worsens during her menstruation and that the pain is "unbearable." She admits that she has had unprotected sex with her boyfriend a few times, but reports that she is taking an oral contraceptive. She denies multiple sexual partners in the past. She has had a few episodes of vomiting and still feels nauseous. No fevers or chills. She also reports pain when having a bowel movement. She denies any vaginal discharge. 

Past Medical History: 
Current medications: Oral Contraceptive
Allergies: None

180.hpi_narrative:
Initial History

Reason(s) for visit: Headache
History of present Illness:
A 55-year-old female with a past medical history of hypertension presents to your office with a an occipital headache, mild vertigo, and a tendency to fall when walking for 6 days. She states that she never had any problems walking or being off-balance. Eight days ago, she stated that she had a pink rash on her arms and torso and felt feverish. The rash improved after a couple days, but the headache and tendency to fall persisted. She had nausea, but she denied any vomiting. She feels weak and "under the weather."  She denies travel, but went hiking 2 weeks ago nearby her house which she routinely does every summer. She denies any history of migraines. She will occasionally get a tension headache which she will treat with Ibuprofen. She has never had a headache that has lasted this long. She denies any trauma to her head. She denies any sick contacts. She denies any recent antibiotic use.  She is very concerned about her symptoms.

PMH:
Past Medical History: Hypertension. The patient recently had a colonoscopy screening which was normal. 
Current medications: HCTZ 25mg PO daily
Allergies: None
Vaccinations: Received Childhood vaccinations.
Women's health: The patient cannot remember when her last pap smear was done.
Family History:
Her father has a history of Hypertension and died of a stroke. Her mother has no health problems and is still living.

Social History:
Marital/Family: She is married with one child. She lives in Gaithersburg, Maryland.
Personal habits: The patient denies smoking. She lives an active lifestyle. She drinks alcohol socially. She denies use of illegal drugs or misuse of medications.
Occupation/educational: She works as a public relations specialist. She is a college graduate with a BS in communication.
Recreational: The patient enjoys to bike and hike. She loves the outdoors and spends as much time as she is able.

Review of systems:
General: See HPI
Skin: See HPI
HEENT: Negative
Cardiorespiratory: Negative
Gastrointestinal: See HPI
Genitourinary: Negative
Neuropsychiatric: See HPI

001.vitalsText: Initial Vital Signs Day 1 @ 16:00 Temperature: 37.0 C (98.6 degrees F) Pulse: 120 beats/min, Weak Respiratory rate: 34 /minute Blood pressure, systolic: 100 mm Hg Blood pressure, diastolic: 60 mm Hg Height: 183cm (72.0 in) Weight: 97.5 kg (215 lb) Body Mass Index: 29.1 kg/m2
exam: General,Well-developed, overweight. He appears in marked respiratory distress. He is moaning and holding his hands over the right side of chest.
Skin,Pale, cool, and diaphoretic. Normal turgor. No lesions. Hair normal.
Heent Neck,Normocephalic. Eyes, ears, nose, and mouth normal. Neck supple; slight tracheal deviation to the left; no masses or bruits; thyroid normal.
Chest Lungs,Chest wall normal. Hyperresonance to percussion on right; no breath sounds. Breath sounds present on the left.
Cardiovascular,Tachycardia; heart sounds faint. No murmurs, rubs, gallops, or extra sounds. Bilateral central and peripheral pulses weak but equal. No jugular venous distention.
Abdomen,Bowel sounds normal; no bruits. No masses or tenderness. Liver and spleen not palpable. No hernias.
Genital,Normal circumcised penis; normal scrotum; testes without masses. No inguinal hernia.
Rectal,Sphincter tone normal. No masses or abnormalities. Prostate normal. Stool brown; no occult blood.

Extremities Spine,Extremities symmetric without deformity, cyanosis, or clubbing. No edema. Bilateral peripheral pulses weak but equal. No joint deformity or warmth; full range of motion. Spine examination normal.
Neuro Psych,Unable to answer questions due to respiratory distress. Deep tendon reflexes normal. Moves all extremities.
001.hpi_narrative:
Reason(s) for visit: Chest pain; respiratory distress

The patient, a 65-year-old accountant, is brought to the emergency department by ambulance from the trucking company, where he works. Ten minutes prior to the ambulance's arrival, the patient developed excruciating, sharp pain on the right side of his chest accompanied by marked respiratory distress. He rates the pain as an 8 on a 10-point scale. The pain increases on respiration, and he is unable to answer questions. A coworker who accompanied the patient to the hospital says that this has never happened to the patient in the past. Coworker mentions patient has a past medical history of emphysema and asthma. Oxygen was administered during transport.

001.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Tension Pneumothorax.

002.title: Altered Mental Status

patient_voice.chief_complaint: I'm really scared. I can't remember what happened.
patient_voice.history: I fell and now I feel confused. I don't know where I am.
patient_voice.pain: My head hurts a lot.

002.vitalsText: Initial Vital Signs Day 1 @ 11:00 Temperature: 36.8 C (98.2 degrees F) Pulse: 88 beats/min. Regular rhythm Respiratory rate: 18 /minute Blood pressure, systolic: 115 mm Hg Blood pressure, diastolic: 85 mm Hg Height: 180cm (70.9 in) Weight: 91.0 kg (200.6 lb) Body Mass Index: 27.9 kg/m2
exam: Confused, follows simple commands; gait unsteady after recent fall
002.hpi_narrative:
Differential: the differential for altered mental status in an elderly patient includes: seizures, bacterial meningitis, urinary tract infection, trauma, electrolyte disturbances, drug or alcohol toxicity, heart failure, metabolic disorders: hypoglycemia, hypercalcemia, uremia, liver failure, thyrotoxicosis.

The patient has a substantial hemorrhage. The clerk is told the patient had a recent fall and has been having episodes of altered mental status since that time. The patient is also at a higher risk for subdural hematomas due to his advanced age and having a recent alcohol intoxication. Especially with falls in elderly, it is important to look for head trauma. CT without contrast is more widely used for the swift turn-around time for results, but MRI is more sensitive in detecting intracranial hemorrhages. Time is of utmost importance in this case as bleeds may cause mass effects that may lead to increased brain damage as time elapses.

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with pain in legs.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
No acute rash; capillary refill and perfusion assessed.
010.hpi_narrative: Intermittent claudication is a condition characterized by pain, cramping, or heaviness in the legs during physical activity, which is relieved by rest. It is caused by insufficient blood flow to the muscles due to arterial occlusion. The patient should be evaluated for risk factors, and appropriate management should be initiated, including lifestyle modifications and possibly revascularization procedures. It is important to assess the severity of the disease and the patient's functional status.

016.hpi_narrative: Intra-abdominal hypertension (IAH) is defined as an intra-abdominal pressure (IAP) greater than 12 mmHg. It is a common complication in critically ill patients, particularly those with trauma, sepsis, or abdominal surgery. IAH can lead to abdominal compartment syndrome (ACS), which can cause organ dysfunction and failure. Early recognition and management of IAH are crucial to prevent progression to ACS. Treatment options include fluid resuscitation, decompression, and monitoring of intra-abdominal pressure.
016.clinical_tip: Until proven otherwise, treat unstable chest pain as ACS.
016.objective: Rule out life threats. ECG within 10 minutes.

Treatment options include fluid resuscitation, decompression, and monitoring of intra-abdominal pressure.

024.hpi_narrative:
Initial History

Reason(s) for visit: Burning during urination
History of present Illness:
The patient, a 19 year old college freshman, presents to your office stating that he has a 5/10, sharp pain when he urinates. The pain stops when urination is complete. The pain began 3 days ago and has been progressively getting worse. He also recently developed testicular pain and pain with sex, especially with ejaculation. He is sexually active with his girlfriend of 6 months, and although they typically use condoms, they occasionally have unprotected sex. He also confirms chills, lethargy, a subjective fever, decreased appetite, but denies nausea and vomiting. Tylenol has improved his pain and fever. 

Past Medical History: Fractured ankle.
Current medications: Tylenol 500mg as needed
Allergies: None
Vaccinations: He received his childhood vaccinations.
Family History: The patient's father has hypertension. His mother has hypothyroidism. 

Social History: 
The patient is a college freshman, and had his first sexual encounter at age 15. He states that he never had a sexually transmitted infection before. He is a social drinker and has experimented with marijuana in the past. He denies any other illicit drug use. He enjoys rock climbing.

Review of systems:
General: See HPI
Skin: Negative
HEENT: Negative
Cardiorespiratory: Negative
Gastrointestinal: Negative
Genitourinary:  See HPI
Neuropsychiatric: Negative

024.objective: Treat infection; rule out pyelonephritis and STI.

exam: Decreased engagement and cognitive change compared with reported baseline.
Altered mental status with attention and command-following documented.
033.hpi_narrative: Differential: Normal pressure hydrocephalus, Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, Subdural hematoma, Dementia, Other causes. Patients with normal pressure hydrocephalus can present with cognitive decline, gait disturbance, and urinary incontinence. The diagnosis is made with neuroimaging, and the treatment is a ventriculoperitoneal shunt. It is important to recognize that normal pressure hydrocephalus is treatable. It was emphasized that the lumbar puncture is the gold standard to diagnose normal pressure hydrocephalus. All of the above patients with these symptoms can be seen in the emergency department. The lumbar puncture is the definitive test for normal pressure hydrocephalus.

044.hpi_narrative: Case Summary: Giardiasis is an infection caused by the parasite Giardia lamblia. It is important to consider this diagnosis in patients presenting with diarrhea, especially if they have traveled recently or have been exposed to contaminated water. The treatment of choice is metronidazole, but other antiparasitic agents will kill Giardia as well. It is also important to ensure that the patient is hydrated, as dehydration can be a significant concern with diarrhea. Additionally, educating the patient about the importance of proper hygiene and avoiding contaminated food and water sources is crucial in preventing future infections.

The treatment of choice is metronidazole, but other antiparasitic agents will kill Giardia as well. It is also important to ensure that the patient is hydrated, as dehydration can be a significant concern with diarrhea. Additionally, educating the patient about the importance of proper hygiene and avoiding contaminated food and water sources is crucial in preventing future infections.

Initial History

Reason(s) for visit: Chest pain; respiratory distress
History of present Illness:
The patient, a 65-year-old accountant, is brought to the emergency department by ambulance from the trucking company, where he works. Ten minutes prior to the ambulance’s arrival, the patient developed excruciating, sharp pain on the right side of his chest accompanied by marked respiratory distress. He rates the pain as an 8 on a 10-point scale. The pain increases on respiration, and he is unable to answer questions. A coworker who accompanied the patient to the hospital says that this has never happened to the patient in the past. Coworker mentions patient has a past medical history of emphysema and asthma. 049.hpi_narrative:
Initial History

Reason(s) for visit: Headache
History of present Illness:
A 55-year-old female with a past medical history of hypertension presents to your office with a an occipital headache, mild vertigo, and a tendency to fall when walking for 6 days. She states that she never had any problems walking or being off-balance. Eight days ago, she stated that she had a pink rash on her arms and torso and felt feverish. The rash improved after a couple days, but the headache and tendency to fall persisted. She had nausea, but she denied any vomiting. She feels weak and "under the weather."  She denies travel, but went hiking 2 weeks ago nearby her house which she routinely does every summer. She denies any history of migraines. She will occasionally get a tension headache which she will treat with Ibuprofen. She has never had a headache that has lasted this long. She denies any trauma to her head. She denies any sick contacts. She denies any recent antibiotic use.  She is very concerned about her symptoms.

PMH:
Past Medical History: Hypertension. The patient recently had a colonoscopy screening which was normal. 
Current medications: HCTZ 25mg PO daily
Allergies: None
Vaccinations: Received Childhood vaccinations.
Women's health: The patient cannot remember when her last pap smear was done.
Family History:
Her father has a history of Hypertension and died of a stroke. Her mother has no health problems and is still living.

Social History:
Marital/Family: She is married with one child. She lives in Gaithersburg, Maryland.
Personal habits: The patient denies smoking. She lives an active lifestyle. She drinks alcohol socially. She denies use of illegal drugs or misuse of medications.
Occupation/educational: She works as a public relations specialist. She is a college graduate with a BS in communication.
Recreational: The patient enjoys to bike and hike. She loves the outdoors and spends as much time as she is able.

Review of systems:
General: See HPI
Skin: See HPI
HEENT: Negative
Cardiorespiratory: Negative
Gastrointestinal: See HPI
Genitourinary: Negative
Neuropsychiatric: See HPI

It is critical to differentiate primary headaches from secondary causes, as this will guide management and treatment. In this case, the patient presented with a classic cluster headache, which is characterized by unilateral, severe pain, often associated with autonomic symptoms. The management of cluster headaches includes abortive and preventive therapies, and understanding the patient's history is essential in tailoring the treatment plan.

054.title: Yellow Baby

patient_voice.chief_complaint: I'm really worried about my baby's jaundice. It looks so yellow.
patient_voice.history: I noticed my baby was getting yellower each day. I’m scared it might be serious.
patient_voice.pain: I just want to make sure my baby is okay.

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with yellow baby.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
Warm skin with fever; no purpura on initial survey.
054.hpi_narrative: Differential diagnosis by the pediatrician. Physiology of hyperbilirubinemia, Gilbert's syndrome, weight, breast milk jaundice, hemolytic disease of the newborn (ABO incompatibility), biliary atresia and G6PD deficiency. The key is to ensure that the baby is feeding well and that the mother is not overfeeding the baby. Although bilirubin levels can be obtained in the laboratory, it is essential for the pediatrician to determine if the infant is feeding well. This is important because if the infant continues to be breastfed the bilirubin levels may continue to rise. It is also important that breastfeeding is encouraged.
054.clinical_tip: Petechiae + fever in a sick patient — treat empirically for meningococcemia.
054.objective: Recognize toxic rash syndromes. Resuscitate and cover infection.

patient_voice.history: I had a cold before. Now my throat hurts and I can't stop coughing.
patient_voice.pain: It hurts when I cough.

exam: Ill-appearing with frequent cough; speaks in short phrases between paroxysms.
058.hpi_narrative:
Differential: Bacterial tracheitis, Epiglottitis, Measles, Pertussis, Bronchopneumonia, abscess, foreign body aspiration, anaphylaxis.

This patient has croup (laryngotracheitis) that most likely stems from respiratory distress. She has the classic findings of croup including a barking cough and respiratory stridor in the setting of recent upper respiratory symptoms. Based on the history and physical exam, she likely has viral croup and is not in respiratory distress. Therefore, further diagnostic testing does not need to be done. In the ED, the patient should receive nebulized epinephrine, dexamethasone (or M.C.M. if whether the patient can tolerate IV access when you are administering IV fluids). Once the patient is given the epinephrine and dexamethasone, the patient will be reevaluated before discharge.

The purpose of this case is to have the user identify a benign condition and restrain from doing unnecessary, dangerous procedures. This patient has a simple tension headache, a very common condition that can be diagnosed clinically and treated as an outpatient. The patient describes certain features including mild to moderate pain which is supported by the physical finding of pericranial and neck muscle tenderness. Otherwise, the exam and vital signs are normal. The user should recognize that unnecessary tests, such as "understanding" identity and acute stress, neurologic deficits, nausea/vomiting, or wanting to sleep in the next hour are not helpful diagnostic to ascertain whether this is a tension headache or not. A CT, MRI, or lumbar puncture is not necessary for tension headaches because the patient has no red flags, as stress is a contributing factor in many patients. The patient will get better with simple NSAID therapy. Alternative treatments for tension headaches include relaxation techniques and trigger point injections. However, there are no restrictive treatments and should only be used after the patient has failed these measures.

067.hpi_narrative: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is the most common benign tumor in men. It is important to recognize that BPH is not a precursor to prostate cancer, although it can lead to urinary symptoms that may mimic those of prostate cancer. 076.title: Fever and Rash

patient_voice.chief_complaint: I'm really scared because my baby has a high fever and a rash.
patient_voice.history: My baby had a fever for days, and now there's a rash. I don't know what to do.
patient_voice.pain: My baby seems uncomfortable and fussy.

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with fever and rash.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Neurologic exam focused on mental status and focal deficits.
Skin rash morphology and distribution documented.
076.hpi_narrative:
Differential: Fifth disease, Measles, Meningitis, Rubella, Scarlet Fever, Drug allergy

This patient has Roseola infantum (exanthem subitum), most frequently caused by human Herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6). The classic presentation for Roseola is in infants 7-13 months old who develop high fevers for 3-5 days (can often cause febrile seizures) that resolve abruptly, followed by the appearance of a macular rash on the neck and torso, spreading to the extremities. Infants are generally well-appearing, active, and after throughout the course of the illness and treatment is mainly supportive (antipyretics for fever, ensuring adequate fluid intake, etc). The main points of this case is to recognize the clinical presentation and make the diagnosis without any diagnostic tests and manage it conservatively without invasive measures.

080.hpi_narrative: This case is a great illustration of the goal with a diagnosis of malrotation. Malrotation occurs as a result of an abnormality of the intestinal gut during embryogenesis. Volvulus occurs when the small bowel twists around itself, causing obstruction. This can lead to ischemia and obstruction. In this case, obstruction was seen by X-rays showing the intestinal loops, and potentially leading to dehydration and necrosis due to the vessels supplying blood to the bowel being cut off. The patient's slow rise in vital signs can lead to severe dehydration as potential hemorrhagic components. The important part of this case is to diagnose the problem quickly and ensure that the diagnosis is made, after which the patient should be stabilized with NG tube decompression and IV fluid resuscitation prior to surgery.

083.hpi_narrative:
Initial History

Reason(s) for visit: Abdominal Pain
History of present Illness:
A 22-year-old female presents to the emergency room with abdominal pain, lethargy, and vomiting x2 days. Her vomiting is non-bloody. Her abdominal pain is diffuse, which she rates as a 6/10. She also claims to have had an increased appetite prior to having these symptoms. She also claims that she’s been developing blurry vision, dizziness, and drowsiness. She also states that she is having increased urination

Past Medical History

Past Medical History: None
Current medications: Birth control
Allergies: None
Vaccinations: The patient received her childhood vaccinations. She has never received any HPV vaccines.
Women's health: The patient cannot remember when her last pap smear was done.
Family History: The patient has a brother with Diabetes. 

Social History:
Marital/Family: Single. She is an undergraduate student at a local university.
Personal habits: The patient denies smoking. She drinks socially. She smoked marijuana "a few times" with her friends. She denies other illicit drugs or misuse of medications. Occupation/educational: She is a student at a local university
Recreational: She plays the piano and sings in a band. 

Review of systems:
General: See HPI
Skin: Her skin is dry. 
HEENT: Her throat is dry. 
Cardiorespiratory: She feels that her heart is beating faster.
Gastrointestinal: See HPI

084.hpi_narrative: The patient is a 67-year-old female who presents with abdominal pain that has been persistent for the last 24 hours. She has a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia. The patient reports that the pain is located in the lower abdomen and is associated with nausea and vomiting. On examination, the patient appears to be in moderate distress. Initial laboratory tests reveal elevated white blood cell count and lactate levels. Imaging studies confirm the diagnosis of ischemic colitis. The patient was admitted for further management and surgical consultation was obtained. It is important to recognize the signs and symptoms of ischemic colitis as it can lead to significant morbidity if not treated promptly.

090.hpi_narrative: Obstetric/Gestational Hypertension: Clinical Presentation and Management. Gestational hypertension is defined as new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks of gestation. The treatment for gestational hypertension includes monitoring blood pressure and, if necessary, initiating antihypertensive therapy. The management of gestational hypertension may include lifestyle modifications and, in some cases, medication.

exam: presents as low back pain that radiates down the leg with perianal and periphrastic numbness and/or loss of bowel and bladder function.

099.hpi_narrative:
Differential: Compression fracture, facet joint degenerative disease, lumbar disk herniation, spinal stenosis, malignancy of the spine.

This patient has cauda equina syndrome. Cauda equina is characterized by the disruption of the cauda equina, the most distal portion of the spinal cord. It typically presents as low back pain that radiates down the leg with perianal and periphrastic numbness and/or loss of bowel and bladder function. Cauda equina syndrome is a medical emergency requiring prompt surgical intervention. Patients suspected of having cauda equina should receive a STAT MRI and neurosurgery consult for spinal decompression. The key to this case is a fast diagnosis with a STAT MRI and a fast consult to neurosurgery. The case will end after neurosurgery sees the patient.

easy.hpi: Differential: Compression fracture, facet joint degenerative disease, lumbar disk herniation, spinal stenosis, malignancy of the spine. This patient has cauda equina syndrome. Cauda equina is characterized by the disruption of the cauda equina, the most distal portion of the spinal cord. It typically presents as low back pain that radiates down the leg with perianal and periphrastic numbness and/or loss of bowel and bladder function. Cauda equina syndrome is a medical emergency requiring prompt surgical intervention. Patients suspected of having cauda equina should receive a STAT MRI and neurosurgery consult for spinal decompression. The key to this case is a fast diagnosis with a STAT MRI and a fast consult to neurosurgery. The case will end after neurosurgery sees the patient.

easy.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Cauda Equina Syndrome. Start with stabilization, then targeted testing.
